title: Given a string and an integer k, find the length of the longest substring you can obtain where all characters are the same after replacing at most k characters. Solve it with the sliding window pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
shortTitle: Longest Substring with Same Letters after Replacement (Longest Repeating Character Replacement)

s1_definition.profdef: This problem asks for the longest window in a string that can be turned into a block of one repeated character by changing at most k of its characters. It is solved with a variable-size sliding window that tracks the frequency of each character inside the window and remembers the highest single-character frequency seen. A window is valid when its length minus that highest frequency is at most k, meaning the remaining non-majority characters can all be replaced. The right pointer expands the window and the left pointer shrinks it only when it becomes invalid.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh reviews a tape of daily risk ratings for an account, each day marked with a single rating letter such as L for low, M for medium, H for high. He is allowed to overturn at most k questionable days to make a cleaner story. He wants the longest continuous streak he can present as a single rating after overturning at most k days. He slides a window across the tape and keeps it only as wide as the rule allows: the window length minus the count of its most common rating must not exceed k.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep the window valid when its length minus the most frequent character count is at most k, and track the widest such window.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem asks for the longest window in a string that can be turned into a block of one repeated character by changing at most k of its characters. It is solved with a variable-size sliding window that tracks the frequency of each character inside the window and remembers the highest single-character frequency seen. A window is valid when its length minus that highest frequency is at most k, meaning the remaining non-majority characters can all be replaced. The right pointer expands the window and the left pointer shrinks it only when it becomes invalid.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh reviews a tape of daily risk ratings for an account, each day marked with a single rating letter such as L for low, M for medium, H for high. He is allowed to overturn at most k questionable days to make a cleaner story. He wants the longest continuous streak he can present as a single rating after overturning at most k days. He slides a window across the tape and keeps it only as wide as the rule allows: the window length minus the count of its most common rating must not exceed k.

**One line to remember:** Keep the window valid when its length minus the most frequent character count is at most k, and track the widest such window.

sections.s2_technical:
We maintain a window with a left and a right boundary and a frequency array or map counting how many times each character appears inside the window. We also keep a running value for the maximum frequency of any single character currently in the window. The key invariant is that a window can be converted into all-identical characters using at most k replacements exactly when the number of characters that are not the majority character, which is the window length minus the maximum frequency, is no more than k.

As the right pointer moves to a new character, we increment that character's frequency and update the maximum frequency with `maxFreq = Math.max(maxFreq, freq[c])`. Then we check validity: if `(right - left + 1) - maxFreq > k`, the window now needs more than k replacements, so we shrink from the left by decrementing the left character's frequency and advancing the left pointer once. We shrink at most one step per expansion because the window only ever grew by one, which keeps the whole scan linear.

A subtle and famous senior-level point is that we do not recompute the maximum frequency when we shrink the window, even though the true maximum might drop. This is intentional and safe. The best answer is driven by the largest valid window we ever achieve, and that window was anchored by the highest maximum frequency we saw. A stale, slightly-too-high maximum frequency can only keep the window from shrinking for a step, but it can never report a window longer than one that was genuinely achievable, so the final answer remains correct while the code stays simple and fast.

The answer is simply the largest window length observed, which equals `right - left + 1` at its widest, and because the left boundary never moves backward we can just return the final window width or track the maximum explicitly. The time complexity is linear, O(n), since each pointer advances at most n times, and the space complexity is O(alphabet size), effectively constant for a fixed character set.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the credit-risk team keeps, for each account, a daily string of risk-rating letters across a review period, one letter per day such as L, M, or H. Regulations let an analyst manually override at most k days inside a review window when documented justification exists. The team wants the longest continuous period they can present as a single uniform rating after using at most k overrides, because a long uniform low-risk stretch supports a credit-limit increase. This is precisely the longest-substring-after-at-most-k-replacements problem.

Problem 2 — Checking every possible period by brute force is quadratic and does not scale to the bank's large account base and long histories. The sliding window with a frequency count and a remembered maximum frequency gives a single linear pass, which is what makes the nightly eligibility recomputation feasible.

The code has the shared `Account` class, a `RiskRatingAnalyzer` service with a `longestUniformRun` method that implements the sliding window, and a runnable `CharacterReplacementDemo` main class that runs Rajesh's and Priya's rating strings with a chosen k, logging each shrink at fine level and the final answer at info level. All classes are normal top-level classes.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's rating string "LLMLHLL" with k equal to 2. We keep a frequency map, a left boundary at 0, a maximum frequency of 0, and a best of 0.

Step 1: Right at index 0, letter L. Frequency of L becomes 1, maximum frequency 1. Window length 1 minus 1 is 0, not greater than 2, valid. Best becomes 1.

Step 2: Right at index 1, letter L. L becomes 2, maximum frequency 2. Length 2 minus 2 is 0, valid. Best becomes 2.

Step 3: Right at index 2, letter M. M becomes 1, maximum frequency stays 2. Length 3 minus 2 is 1, at most 2, valid. Best becomes 3.

Step 4: Right at index 3, letter L. L becomes 3, maximum frequency 3. Length 4 minus 3 is 1, valid. Best becomes 4.

Step 5: Right at index 4, letter H. H becomes 1, maximum frequency stays 3. Length 5 minus 3 is 2, at most 2, valid. Best becomes 5.

Step 6: Right at index 5, letter L. L becomes 4, maximum frequency 4. Length 6 minus 4 is 2, valid. Best becomes 6.

Step 7: Right at index 6, letter L. L becomes 5, maximum frequency 5. Length 7 minus 5 is 2, valid. Best becomes 7. Wait, the string length is only 7 characters, and window 0 to 6 is the whole string; the two non-L letters M and H can both be overridden with k equal to 2, so the best is 7? The string "LLMLHLL" has exactly two non-L letters, so with k equal to 2 the entire length 7 is achievable, and best is 7.

The final longest uniform run for Rajesh is 7 because the only two non-low ratings can both be overridden.

```

2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Longest uniform rating run with k=2 overrides = 7
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Rajesh Kumar best uniform run = 7
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Priya Sharma (CUR3001) ratings=HMHMHMM
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Longest uniform rating run with k=2 overrides = 5
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
This problem asks for the longest substring I can turn into a block of a single repeated character by changing at most k of its characters, and I solve it with a variable-size sliding window in linear time. Inside the window I keep a frequency count of each character and I track the highest single-character frequency I have seen. The window is valid exactly when its length minus that highest frequency is at most k, because that difference is the number of non-majority characters I would need to replace. I expand the right pointer over each character, update the frequency and the running maximum, and whenever the window becomes invalid I shrink it by one from the left.

The detail that separates a strong answer here is that I deliberately do not recompute the maximum frequency when the window shrinks. That might feel wrong at first, but it is both safe and the reason the code stays clean. The final answer is driven by the widest valid window I ever reach, and a slightly stale maximum can only delay a shrink by a step; it can never produce a window wider than one that was genuinely achievable, so correctness holds while the scan stays strictly linear.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on the credit-risk team. For each account we stored a daily string of risk-rating letters, and regulators allowed analysts to override at most k documented days within a review window. We computed the longest continuous period that could be presented as a single uniform rating after those overrides, because a long uniform low-risk stretch supported raising a customer's credit limit. The linear window let us recompute eligibility across the whole account base in the nightly batch.

The senior-level point I make is that this is a sliding window where the validity test is length minus the most frequent count against k, and recognizing that framing is what turns a confusing word problem into a two-pointer template. I also mention that I use a fixed-size integer array instead of a hash map when the rating alphabet is small, which removes boxing overhead and matters when the job runs over very long histories, and that the whole thing is linear time and constant extra space. That combination of a correctness insight plus a performance choice is what interviewers want to hear.
